01.event: A large mortar in his house was placed against the door
01.outcome: Ruled it has the status of a utensil
01.summary: Mar Shmuel had a large mortar in his house and permitted it to be placed against the door, ruling that it counts as a utensil.
01.missing: Any event beyond the ruling; no response, change or consequence.
01.reason: A bare report of a rabbi's permission cited as a legal precedent; nothing happens beyond the ruling.

02.event: He habitually bent down so his mother could step on him to climb in and out of bed
02.turn: He boasted of it in the study hall
02.outcome: The sages told him he had not reached half the honor due, citing a mother who threw a purse into the sea
02.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would bend down so his mother could use him as a step to get into and out of bed. He came and praised himself for this in the study hall. The sages deflated him: he had not reached even half the honor due to a mother.
02.reason: A habitual practice leads to a one-time event (his boasting in the study hall) and a pointed response that reverses his self-assessment; there are actions and a change, not mere speech.

03.event: She came to Rabbi Yehuda's court
03.turn: People there told her to lament, tear her clothes and unbind her hair
03.outcome: Not stated; the Gemara discusses why they advised her so
03.summary: A woman came to Rabbi Yehuda's court to testify her husband had died, and those present told her to display mourning so she would be believed. The Gemara then asks whether they taught her to lie.
03.missing: What she did, and what the court ruled.
03.reason: Coming before the court is the only event; the rest is advice and the Gemara's discussion, with no narrated outcome or change.

04.missing: An incident; the passage is a legal argument citing a general historical fact.
04.reason: The re-circumcisions in the days of ben Koziva are cited as a general fact in a halakhic debate, not narrated as an event.

05.actor: Rabbi Abbahu (or Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba), Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
05.event: He sat and taught a ruling in Rabbi Yohanan's name
05.turn: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turned their faces away in silent disagreement
05.outcome: Nothing further; Rav Pappa explains why they did not speak
05.summary: Rabbi Abbahu taught that the halakha follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka in Rabbi Yohanan's name, and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turned their faces away in protest. The Gemara gives an alternate version and Rav Pappa explains their silence by deference to Caesar's court.
05.missing: Any consequence of the gesture; it serves as evidence in a legal question.
05.reason: Mainly speech, with one non-verbal act of protest that signals conflict; nothing follows, so it is at most borderline.

06.actor: A man who betrothed a woman conditionally; the Sages
06.event: He betrothed conditionally and then had relations with her
06.turn: The Sages could not release her without a bill of divorce
06.summary: Ulla's ruling is supported by a real incident: a man betrothed a woman conditionally and then lived with her, and the Sages lacked the power to let her go without a bill of divorce.
06.missing: The incident is only alluded to; the details are supplied by the translation.
06.reason: An incident cited as evidence and only alluded to, which a reader must fill in; R-C6 makes this borderline.

07.turn: A bone was found between her teeth
07.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again
07.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house immersed and emerged, and a bone was found between her teeth. Rabbi required her to immerse again.
07.reason: There is an event and a discovery followed by a ruling that changes her status, but it is a brief precedent cited inside a legal challenge with little development.

08.event: Rav Yosef said he had not heard a halakha
08.turn: Abaye reminded him that he himself had taught it
08.summary: Rav Yosef said he had never heard a teaching, and his student Abaye reminded him that he had taught it to them himself, with three inferences.
08.missing: Any event beyond speech; his illness is only in the translator's gloss.
08.reason: Purely a scholarly exchange of speech with no real conflict or event.

09.actor: Rava Tosfa'a; a woman whose husband went overseas
09.event: Her husband went abroad and she gave birth twelve months later
09.turn: The case came before Rava Tosfa'a
09.summary: A woman's husband went overseas and she gave birth twelve months after he left. Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child legitimate, and the Gemara asks whose opinion he followed.
09.missing: Detail of the incident; it is cited as a precedent in the discussion.
09.reason: There are events (departure, late birth) and a ruling that changes the child's status, but it is a terse precedent embedded in legal argument.

10.actor: A man whose betrothed died; Rav Nahman, Ulla, Avimei, Rav Hiyya bar Ami
10.event: The man came before the seated rabbis
10.turn: They told him to bury her or pay her ketubah; Rav Hiyya objected with a baraita
10.summary: Several rabbis were sitting when a man whose betrothed had died came before them; they told him to bury her or pay her ketubah, and Rav Hiyya bar Ami objected citing a baraita.
10.missing: Any action or change beyond coming before the rabbis and their ruling.
10.reason: One event (coming before the rabbis) followed by a ruling and discussion with nothing changing, which Jeff ruled is not a story.

11.actor: Rav Yehezkel, his son Rav Yehuda, Shmuel
11.event: Rav Yehezkel taught a mishna to his son Rami
11.turn: Rav Yehuda corrected his father's version
11.outcome: Shmuel rebuked Rav Yehuda for speaking to his father that way
11.summary: Rav Yehezkel taught a mishna, his son Rav Yehuda told him not to teach it that way and they argued it out. Shmuel later rebuked Rav Yehuda for speaking so to his father.
11.reason: All dialogue and scholarly debate with a rebuke; ordinary rabbinic back-and-forth, no event beyond speaking.

12.missing: An incident; this is an exegetical inference about the Israelites.
12.reason: A fragment of exegesis about biblical events, not a narrated story.

13.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna; Rav Huna asked to meet him
13.turn: Rav Hamnuna came without a head covering and admitted he was unmarried
13.outcome: Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to see his face until he married
13.summary: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna, who asked to see him. When Rav Hamnuna came, Rav Huna saw he wore no head cloth and learned he was unmarried. Rav Huna turned his face away and barred him from his presence until he married.
13.reason: Several actions (praise, arrival, seeing, turning away) with conflict and a change in their relationship; more than speech.

14.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
14.event: They bought a maidservant and left silver as collateral for want of coins
14.turn: Her price rose and the sellers wanted to back out
14.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled no acquisition had taken place
14.summary: Rav Huna bar Avin's sons bought a maidservant for perutot but, lacking the money, left a piece of silver. Her price then rose, and they came before Rabbi Ami, who ruled there was neither payment nor collateral, so no sale.
14.reason: Matches the cow shape: several narrated actions and a change (the price rise) before a ruling resolves it.

15.missing: Any event beyond a question and answer.
15.reason: Students ask Rabbi Eliezer a question and he answers; a question and answer is not a story (Yevamot 78b:9).

16.event: In his days there was a bread he threw to his dog
16.turn: The dog would not eat it
16.outcome: Cited as proof the bread is inedible
16.summary: In Mar Shmuel's time there was a bread so bad that when he threw it to his dog, even the dog would not eat it.
16.missing: Context or development; it is cited as evidence in a halakhic objection.
16.reason: Two small events with a result, but alluded to as evidence with little causality or change; at most borderline.

17.event: She meant to invite her friend to eat milk
17.turn: Her mispronunciation made it a curse
17.summary: A Galilean woman meant to offer her neighbor milk but, mispronouncing, said may a lioness eat you.
17.missing: Any event beyond speech or any consequence.
17.reason: A speech-only anecdote illustrating poor pronunciation, with no conflict or event.

18.missing: A one-time event; it is a rabbi's practice and reason.
18.reason: Mareimar's practice of closing Sura's alleyways with nets is a bare report of a custom that leads nowhere.

19.actor: Bar Shatya; two pairs of witnesses; Rav Ashi
19.event: Bar Shatya, who was intermittently insane, sold property
19.turn: Two pairs of witnesses contradicted each other on his sanity at the sale
19.outcome: Rav Ashi ruled the testimonies cancel and the land stays with Bar Shatya
19.summary: Bar Shatya, who sometimes went insane, sold land. One pair of witnesses said he sold while sane and another said while insane. Rav Ashi ruled the testimonies cancel and the land remains in Bar Shatya's possession.
19.reason: A real incident with actions (the sale, conflicting testimony) resolved by a ruling, but cited tersely as a legal proof with little development.

20.event: Seven teachings were said Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura
20.turn: They were repeated that same afternoon before Rava in Pumbedita
20.outcome: Cited as proof about Shabbat limits
20.summary: Seven teachings said on Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura were repeated before Rava in Pumbedita by the end of the same Shabbat, though the distance could not be walked.
20.missing: Who carried them and how; the incident is only alluded to.
20.reason: An incident alluded to as evidence in a legal argument, needing context to fill in; R-C6 makes it borderline.
